lead: An aircraft knows its speed and height by measuring pressure. A pitot tube faces the airflow and senses total pressure; a static port on the side senses the surrounding pressure. Their difference drives the airspeed indicator, while static pressure alone drives the altimeter. Both are simple mechanical computers, but their readings depend on calibration and on the pressure setting the pilot chooses. Pilots use them every take-off, climb, cruise and landing, from a short circuit to a long-haul cruise, so reading them correctly is a core cockpit skill.
prereq: You need basic pressure and density ideas from physics; no earlier chapter is needed.

sections.h3: Pitot-static ports and the airspeed indicator

blocks.text: A pitot tube points into the relative airflow. Its open end brings air to rest and senses total pressure P<sub>0</sub>. A static port sits flush on the fuselage side and senses the surrounding static pressure P. The difference is impact pressure q:
q = P<sub>0</sub> − P = ½ ρ V²
blocks.where: q is impact pressure in Pa; P<sub>0</sub> is total pressure in Pa; P is static pressure in Pa; ρ is air density in kg/m³; V is the speed for which that impact pressure is produced at density ρ.

blocks.text: q = ½ρV² holds for incompressible flow, roughly below Mach 0.3 (about 200 kt at sea level); at higher speed the airspeed indicator needs a compressibility correction.

In the airspeed indicator, a thin capsule feels P<sub>0</sub> on one side and P on the other. It expands with q, and a linkage moves the needle. The dial is calibrated at sea-level ISA density, ρ<sub>0</sub> = 1.225 kg/m³. Rearranging q = ½ρV² gives V = √(2q/ρ). Because the dial is calibrated at ρ<sub>0</sub>, a given q always shows the same indicated speed. In thin air ρ is smaller, so the same q is produced by a higher true speed: TAS is greater than IAS, and the gap grows with altitude.

The dial shows indicated airspeed (IAS). Calibrated airspeed (CAS) is IAS corrected for position and installation error. True airspeed (TAS) is CAS corrected for air density, and at high Mach number also for compressibility. The coloured arcs are IAS limits: white for flap operation, green for normal, yellow for caution, and the red radial for never-exceed speed V<sub>ne</sub>.

The altimeter uses a sealed aneroid capsule with a near vacuum inside. As static pressure falls, the capsule expands; as pressure rises, it compresses. A linkage turns the pointer. The static port is its only pressure input, so a blocked static line freezes the reading.

The subscale knob sets the reference pressure in the small window. Set QNH, the aerodrome pressure reduced to sea level, and on the ground the altimeter reads aerodrome elevation. Set 1013.25 hPa and it reads pressure altitude. Near sea level, h ≈ (P<sub>ref</sub> − P) × 27 ft/hPa; P<sub>ref</sub> is the set pressure, P is outside static pressure and h is height.

Pressure altitude is not true altitude. ISA pressure falls about 1 hPa per 27 ft near sea level and temperature falls 6.5 °C/km. In air colder than ISA, pressure levels are compressed and the aircraft is lower than the altimeter says. Flying from high pressure to low pressure also makes the altimeter overread.

No pressure instrument is perfect. Position error comes from airflow around the ports and changes with angle of attack and flap. Leaks make readings sluggish or wrong. Lag delays the response. Temperature error matters most for the altimeter. Blockage is the dangerous one. Some pressure-sensing chains also appear in fuel quantity indication, see 3.13.

items: Pitot blocked, static clear: in a climb the trapped P<sub>0</sub> stays fixed while P falls, so q rises and the ASI overreads; in a descent it underreads.
Static blocked: the ASI, altimeter and VSI lose their true source; the ASI may behave like an altimeter, the altimeter freezes, and the VSI reads zero.
Pitot heat is the cure for ice in the pitot tube; it does not clear a blocked static port, so check the static drains.
Before flight, remove covers, check ports and drain holes, and cross-check the ASI at the runway.

spec.title: Pitot-static feeds to the three pressure instruments
spec.aria: The pitot port feeds only the airspeed capsule, while the static port feeds the airspeed capsule, the altimeter capsule and the vertical speed indicator.

examples.question: (a) At sea level, where air density is 1.225 kg/m³, an aircraft has an impact pressure of 2500 Pa. Find the indicated airspeed in m/s and in knots. Use 1 m/s = 1.94384 kt. (b) The altimeter subscale is set to 1013.25 hPa and the static pressure outside is 950 hPa. Find the pressure altitude, using 27 ft per hPa.
examples.answer: The airspeed is about 63.9 m/s (124 kt), and the pressure altitude is about 1708 ft (roughly 1710 ft).
examples.check:
import math
rho = 1.225
q = 2500.0
V = math.sqrt(2 * q / rho)
V_kt = V * 1.94384
dp = 1013.25 - 950.0
alt = dp * 27.0
print(round(V, 1))
print(round(V_kt, 1))
print(round(dp, 2))
print(round(alt, 1))

traps: Mixing up the ports: the pitot port feeds only the airspeed capsule, while the static port feeds the airspeed capsule, altimeter and vertical speed indicator.
Reading indicated airspeed as true airspeed. At altitude, the same IAS corresponds to a higher TAS because the air density is lower.
Forgetting that the altimeter reads height above the pressure level set in its subscale, not height above the ground or above sea level unless QNH is set correctly.
Thinking a blocked pitot always makes the ASI read zero. With static pressure still changing, a blocked pitot can make the ASI climb when the aircraft climbs.
Using 1013.25 hPa as QNH for landing. It gives pressure altitude; QNH must come from the aerodrome pressure report.

quiz.q: State what the pitot port and the static port sense.
quiz.a: The pitot port senses total pressure P<sub>0</sub>. The static port senses static pressure P.

quiz.q: Why does the same indicated airspeed at a higher altitude correspond to a higher true airspeed?
quiz.a: The ASI is calibrated for sea-level density. At altitude the air density is lower, so a given impact pressure q corresponds to a higher true speed through V = √(2q/ρ).

quiz.q: An aircraft at sea level has q = 3600 Pa and ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Find the indicated airspeed in m/s.
The pitot tube is blocked by ice but the static port is clear. The aircraft climbs. Explain what the ASI shows and why it is unsafe.
quiz.a: The trapped P<sub>0</sub> stays fixed while static pressure P falls during the climb. Since q = P<sub>0</sub> − P, q rises and the ASI indication increases, even though the actual airspeed may be falling. The pilot cannot trust the ASI.

quiz.q: Which pressure is set in the altimeter subscale to read pressure altitude?
Why does the altimeter have a subscale knob?
quiz.a: The knob sets the reference pressure so the altimeter reads height above the chosen pressure datum, such as QNH for elevation or 1013.25 hPa for pressure altitude.

quiz.q: The altimeter subscale is set to 1013 hPa and the outside static pressure is 980 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, find the pressure altitude.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern aircraft digitise pitot and static pressures in an air data computer, which outputs airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and temperature to displays and data buses; see Unit 4, Avionics Architecture, Displays and Data Buses. QNH and pressure altitude also matter in reduced vertical separation minima airspace, where altimeters must be accurate and cross-checked. Cold-temperature altimetry and blocked-pitot accidents are standard safety study topics. Search for air data module, RVSM altimetry, and unreliable airspeed procedures.
